title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: Mrs. Dashwood called on Lady Middleton the next day, taking two of her daughters with her. Marianne excused herself on some slight pretext of work to be done. Her mother assumed that Willoughby had promised the previous evening to visit while the others were out, and was perfectly happy for her to stay at home.

On returning from the park, they found Willoughby’s curricle and servant waiting outside the cottage. Mrs. Dashwood felt certain her guess had been correct. So far, everything was as she had expected. But inside the house she encountered something no foresight had prepared her for. They had scarcely entered the passage when Marianne hurried out of the parlour in obvious distress, holding a handkerchief to her eyes. Without acknowledging them, she ran upstairs. Surprised and alarmed, they went straight into the room she had left. Willoughby was there alone, leaning against the mantelpiece with his back to them. He turned as they entered, and his face showed that he shared much of the emotion that had overwhelmed Marianne.
“What is wrong with her?” Mrs. Dashwood exclaimed as she entered. “Is she unwell?”
“I hope not,” he answered, attempting to look cheerful. Then, with a forced smile, he added, “It is I who have more reason to expect to be ill. I am suffering a very great disappointment!”
“A disappointment?”

“Yes. I cannot keep my engagement with you. This morning Mrs. Smith has used the privilege of wealth to send a poor dependent cousin to London on business. I have just received my instructions and said goodbye at Allenham. Now, to cheer myself up, I have come to say goodbye to you.”
“To London! Are you leaving this very morning?”
“Almost at this very moment.”
“How unfortunate. Still, Mrs. Smith must be obliged. I hope her business will not keep you away from us for long.”
He reddened as he answered, “You are very kind, but I do not expect to return to Devonshire soon. I never visit Mrs. Smith more than once within a year.”
“And is Mrs. Smith your only friend? Is Allenham the only house nearby where you would be welcome? For shame, Willoughby! Surely you do not wait to be invited here?”
He grew still redder. Looking down at the floor, he answered only, “You are much too kind.”
Mrs. Dashwood looked at Elinor in surprise. Elinor was equally astonished. For a few moments nobody spoke. Mrs. Dashwood was the first to break the silence.

“I can only add, my dear Willoughby, that you will always be welcome at Barton Cottage. I shall not urge you to return immediately, since only you can judge how far that would please Mrs. Smith. On that point, I am no more inclined to question your judgment than to doubt your wishes.”
“My present commitments,” Willoughby replied in confusion, “are of a kind that—that I dare not hope—”

He broke off. Mrs. Dashwood was too astonished to answer, and another silence followed. Willoughby ended it with a faint smile. “It is foolish to linger like this. I will not torment myself any further by staying among friends whose company I cannot now enjoy.”
He hurriedly said goodbye to them all and left the room. They watched him get into his carriage, and within a minute it had disappeared from sight.
Mrs. Dashwood was too overcome to speak. She immediately left the parlour to give way in private to the distress and alarm his abrupt departure had caused.

Elinor was at least as uneasy as her mother. She considered what had just happened with anxiety and suspicion. Willoughby’s manner at parting, his embarrassment and pretended cheerfulness, and above all his reluctance to accept her mother’s invitation disturbed her deeply. That hesitation was so unlike a lover, so unlike himself. One moment she feared he had never intended anything serious; the next, that some unhappy quarrel had taken place between him and Marianne. A serious quarrel would most readily explain the distress in which her sister had left the room. Yet when Elinor considered the strength of Marianne’s love, a quarrel seemed almost impossible.

Whatever the details of their parting, there could be no doubt of her sister’s suffering. Elinor thought with the tenderest compassion of the violent grief Marianne was probably not only yielding to for relief, but nurturing and encouraging as a duty.
About half an hour later, her mother returned. Her eyes were red, but her expression was not without cheerfulness.
“Our dear Willoughby must be several miles from Barton by now, Elinor,” she said, sitting down to her sewing. “And how heavy his heart must be as he travels!”

“It is all so strange. To leave so suddenly! It seems to have happened in an instant. Only last night he was here, so happy, cheerful, and affectionate. And now, with barely ten minutes’ warning—gone, and with no intention of returning! Something more must have happened than he admitted. He neither spoke nor behaved like himself. You must have noticed the difference as clearly as I did. What can explain it? Could they have quarrelled? Why else was he so unwilling to accept your invitation?”

“He did not lack the wish to accept, Elinor. I could see that plainly. He was not able to do so. I assure you, I have considered it all, and can explain perfectly everything that seemed strange to me at first, just as it did to you.”
“Can you really explain it!”

“Yes. I have found a thoroughly satisfactory explanation. But you, Elinor, like to doubt wherever possible. I know it will not satisfy you; still, you will not persuade me to give up my confidence in it. I am convinced Mrs. Smith suspects his love for Marianne and disapproves, perhaps because she has other plans for him. That is why she wants him away. The business she has sent him to conduct is merely an excuse to dismiss him. That is what I believe has happened. He also knows that she disapproves of the connection, and therefore dare not tell her at present that he is engaged to Marianne. Because he depends on her, he feels obliged to submit to her plans and stay away from Devonshire for a time. You will tell me, I know, that this may or may not be what happened. But I shall hear no objections unless you can offer another explanation as satisfactory as this one. Now, Elinor, what do you say?”
“Nothing. You have already supplied the answer I would have given.”

“So you would have said it may or may not have happened. Oh, Elinor, I cannot understand your feelings! You would rather believe evil without proof than good. You would rather look for misery for Marianne and guilt in poor Willoughby than find an excuse for him. You are determined to blame him because his farewell was less affectionate than his usual behaviour. Will you make no allowance for thoughtlessness, or for spirits lowered by a recent disappointment? Must we reject probabilities simply because they are not certainties? Do we owe nothing to a man we have every reason to love and no reason in the world to mistrust? Nothing to the possibility of motives perfectly defensible in themselves, although necessarily secret for a while? And after all, what do you suspect him of?”

“I can scarcely tell you myself. But when someone changes as much as we have just seen him change, suspicion of something unpleasant is inevitable. Still, there is a great deal of truth in what you say about making allowances for him. I wish to judge everyone fairly. Willoughby may certainly have very good reasons for his behaviour, and I shall hope he has. But it would have been more like him to admit them openly. Secrecy may be wise; nevertheless, I cannot help wondering at his being the one to practise it.”
“Then do not blame him for acting against his nature when it is necessary. But you really do admit that what I have said in his defence is fair? I am happy, then, and he is acquitted.”

“Not completely. It may be wise to hide their engagement—if they are engaged—from Mrs. Smith. If so, Willoughby may have very good reason to spend little time in Devonshire just now. But that does not excuse their hiding it from us.”
“Hiding it from us! My dear child, are you accusing Willoughby and Marianne of concealment? How very strange, when every day your looks have reproached them for being too open.”
“I need no proof that they love each other,” Elinor said. “But I do need proof of their engagement.”
“I am entirely satisfied on both points.”
“Yet neither of them has said a single word to you on the subject.”

“I have needed no words when their actions have spoken so clearly. For at least the past fortnight, has his behaviour to Marianne and to all of us not shown that he loves her and regards her as his future wife? Has he not shown us the affection of the closest relation? Have we not understood each other perfectly? Have his looks, his manner, his attentive and affectionate respect not asked for my consent every day? My Elinor, how can you doubt their engagement? How could the thought even enter your mind? Willoughby must be certain of your sister’s love. How can you imagine him leaving her, perhaps for months, without telling her of his own affection? How could they part without confiding in each other?”

“I admit,” Elinor replied, “that everything except one circumstance supports their being engaged. But that one circumstance is their complete silence about it, and to me it nearly outweighs all the others.”

“How strange! You must think very badly of Willoughby if, after everything we have openly witnessed between them, you can doubt the nature of their relationship. Has he been acting a part towards your sister all this time? Do you really suppose he feels nothing for her?”
“No, I cannot believe that. He must love her, and I am sure he does.”
“Then it is a peculiar sort of love, if he can leave her with the indifference and disregard for the future that you attribute to him.”

“You must remember, my dear mother, that I have never treated this as certain. I admit I have had doubts, but they are weaker now and may soon disappear entirely. If we find that they write to one another, all my fears will be removed.”

“What an immense concession! If you saw them at the altar, you would suppose they were about to be married. Ungenerous girl! I need no such proof. In my opinion, nothing has happened to justify doubt. They have attempted no secrecy; everything has been consistently open and unreserved. You cannot question your sister’s wishes, so it must be Willoughby you suspect. But why? Is he not a man of honour and feeling? Has he behaved inconsistently in any way that gives cause for alarm? Could he be deceitful?”

“I hope not; I believe not,” Elinor exclaimed. “I love Willoughby, truly love him. Doubting his honesty cannot hurt you more than it hurts me. The suspicion came without my wishing it, and I shall not encourage it. I admit the change in his manner this morning startled me. He did not speak like himself, or answer your kindness with any warmth. But the circumstances you imagine could explain it all. He had just parted from my sister and seen her leave him in terrible distress. If fear of offending Mrs. Smith obliged him to resist the temptation of returning soon, while he knew that refusing your invitation and announcing a long absence would make his conduct towards our family seem ungenerous and suspicious, he might understandably be embarrassed and troubled. In that case, I think a clear, honest admission of his difficulties would have done him more credit and better suited his usual character. But I will not criticise someone’s conduct on so ungenerous a basis as their judging differently from me, or departing from what I consider right and consistent.”

“You speak very properly. Willoughby certainly does not deserve suspicion. We have not known him long, but he is no stranger in this neighbourhood. Who has ever said anything against him? If he were free to act independently and marry at once, leaving without openly acknowledging everything to me might have been odd. But he is not. In some ways the engagement has begun under difficult circumstances, since the date of their marriage must be very uncertain. Even secrecy, so far as it can be preserved, may now be extremely wise.”

Margaret’s arrival interrupted their conversation, leaving Elinor free to think over all the explanations her mother had offered, acknowledge how probable many of them were, and hope that every one was correct.

They did not see Marianne until dinner. She entered and took her seat without a word. Her eyes were red and swollen, and even then she seemed scarcely able to hold back her tears. She avoided everyone’s gaze and could neither eat nor speak. After a while her mother silently pressed her hand with tender sympathy. What little firmness Marianne had gave way entirely; she burst into tears and left the room.

This overwhelming misery lasted all evening. She had no power to control herself because she had no wish to do so. The smallest reference to anything connected with Willoughby instantly overcame her. Her family attended anxiously to her comfort, but unless they remained completely silent, they could not avoid every subject her feelings linked with him.
